candidateDecisions.label: Climate, sustainability and environmental science with economics and policy
Human rights, international law and global justice

analysis: The closest programme combines sociology, history, international relations, public international law, psychology, public health and environmental governance to study how global change affects local communities. It offers introductory Dutch and substantive work on exclusion, legal protection and conflict, with limited dedicated migration, religion, anthropology and education study. The Environment & Economy theme supports a distinct route with fifteen different courses in each direction, including a sustained Earth science and sustainability sequence, public economics and climate communication. A further justice route would reuse the closest plan’s international law, rights, ethics and conflict courses. The additional criminal, private, constitutional and EU law courses would change the course list without deepening the evidenced global justice questions. The other eight foreign languages have no corresponding planned UCR course sequence, and a single introductory Dutch course contributes only to the broad comparison. The shared data and statistics courses supply transferable quantitative methods. In the broad option qualitative interviews and field research complement sociology and international law. The Dutch course covers introductory communication. Ethics and social psychology contribute moral and empirical perspectives to belief and exclusion. The environmental option combines substantial mitigation, biogeochemistry, biodiversity, resource recovery and energy studies with market failures, climate justice and governance. The early team research course retains its contribution of applied investigation with Zeeland partners, and is complementary to the Maastricht field study and individual thesis. Keep specialised field, learning and language components separate. Public international law includes refugee protection and provides a partial rather than full migration-policy match.

alignment.rationale: Both develop academic reading, writing, reflection and interpersonal skills. Maastricht embeds these in global citizenship and problem-based learning; the credits and scope differ.
Both teach inferential statistics, estimation and hypothesis testing. UCR provides a general methods foundation; Maastricht applies statistics to environmental and economic datasets.
Both develop practical data analysis and visualisation. UCR develops these skills through exploratory projects with varied datasets.
Both address policy tools for environmental problems and the roles of public and private actors. Maastricht integrates climate science and economics; UCR concentrates on sustainability governance.

Refugee law provides a specific overlap with Maastricht’s legal categories and mobility channels. UCR is a broad public-international-law course; Maastricht integrates economics, psychology and the full migration trajectory.

Both analyse conflict and ways to build peaceful societies. Maastricht combines this with justice and preparation for the field study; UCR focuses on conflict causation, transformation and peacebuilding.

Both examine how social processes connect people and societies. Sociology supplies a disciplinary foundation; Maastricht explicitly integrates theories and histories of globalisation across disciplines.

Both develop qualitative research design and data analysis in a research project. Maastricht specifically trains semi-structured migration interviews; UCR offers a broader qualitative research process.

Both provide language study when Dutch is selected as a non-native language. UCR’s single introductory Dutch course does not reproduce the four-semester Maastricht language track or its level requirement.
Both examine environmental discourse. UCR analyses texts, media and public arguments about climate change, while Maastricht teaches discourse analysis as a research method.
